headline_marked: PHP CVE-2026-115560: [[Unpatched RCE Risk]] from Serialization Handler Switching and Upload Progress
headline: PHP CVE-2026-115560: Unpatched RCE Risk from Serialization Handler Switching and Upload Progress
summary: A newly identified PHP vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560) poses an unpatched Remote Code Execution risk under specific, rare configurations involving session.serialize_handler switching and enabled upload progress. Users are advised to verify application code pat
details: The PHP project has announced a potential Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, stemming from a rare combination of configurations. This risk arises when session.serialize_handler is switched at runtime and session upload progress remains enabled.

Specifically, the vulnerability occurs if session.serialize_handler changes from php_binary or php_serialize to php while session_start() is called and upload progress is active. This scenario is not applicable to all standard PHP environments, requiring specific code patterns.

No patched version is currently available for this vulnerability. Organizations running public-facing PHP applications should immediately search their code for combinations of session.serialize_handler, ini_set, and session_start.

Temporary mitigations include disabling upload progress and restarting workers until the application's affected status is determined. This notice is based on advance information from the PHP project and is not a report of successful compromise in production.

headline_marked: [[Abandoned Popcorn Time apps disabled]] to prevent millions of devices joining a botnet
headline: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps disabled to prevent millions of devices joining a botnet
summary: Security researchers took over inactive domains to push a self-disabling update to the 'Netflix of Piracy' software, which was still running on Windows, macOS, and Android devices.
details: Popcorn Time, the popular torrent streaming app from the 2010s, has been abandoned by its developers for years. However, a fork called "Time4Popcorn" continued to run an outdated updater on millions of devices globally.

Researchers at Eye Security discovered that this updater was phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP. It was also running an insecure version of Chrome, creating a significant vulnerability.

The flaw meant that anyone taking over these domains could install virtually any software with full privileges on affected devices. This presented a clear risk for creating botnets, performing man-in-the-middle attacks, or conducting surveillance.
Eye Security's solution involved registering one of the abandoned domains and using it to send a custom update. This update instructed the vulnerable updater to disable itself, mitigating the risk.

Despite ethical concerns about pushing an unsolicited update, the researchers stated that the only alternative was to do nothing. They argued the update process was non-functional and only posed a risk to users.

For Windows devices, the update simply stopped and disabled the service via the Service Control Manager without deleting files. On macOS, a shell script blocked the update process from starting; Android devices were not addressed due to requiring user interaction for updates.

An initial version of their update was flagged as malware by VirusTotal, causing security programs to block it and leave the vulnerable updater active. Eye Security had to tweak the update to bypass this issue.
By March, Eye Security had sent out over 2 million update downloads before stopping the process. They then transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.
